The v5 numbers (14 real against 35 upside-down) stay the reference; v7 gives 14 against 32 for the same half.

docs.title: Questions
docs.text:
1. Why did we count shared stars before planning a benchmark?

A comparison is only fair where both searches looked at the same stars with the same data. With 30 shared stars, the test is small, and that shapes what we can conclude.

2. Running a GPL program on your data is not the same as copying its code into yours. Why does that matter for our licence plan?

The share-alike rule bites when code is combined into another program. Running their tool separately and citing it keeps our own code free to be MIT. This is likely but not legal advice.

3. A tool takes about 50 millionths of a second per star. Why does that not make it the better choice for 549 stars?

Speed matters against the size of the job. Ours already finishes in about 40 minutes, so the limit on what we find is how well we test and vet events, not how fast we compute.

4. A fake dip is found 61% of the time, and 80% of the ones found pass the checks. What share does the search keep?

About 49% (0.61 times 0.80). Quote both numbers, because a figure that only counts the dips that were found hides how many were never found.

5. A paper says one method, the code uses another. What do you do before building a benchmark?

Read the code too, then decide whether you are testing the paper's method or the repository's. The two can give different numbers.

6. mono-cbp found 437 events and we found 41 on the same stars. Why is that not a result about which tool is better?

The tools count different things: their strength scale is different, they search to much weaker dips, and their strongest events look like leftover eclipses. Only 3 events overlapped. A fixed answer, like a known planet, is a fairer judge than a count.

7. Our PDCSAP input found 4 of 8 TOI-1338 b transits and SAP found 7 of 8. What do you do with that?

Do not swap one for the other: either alone finds all 8 only when combined, because they fail in different sectors. Queue a change to search both and keep the union, record which product saw each event, and re-prove that the old numbers are unchanged before freezing it.

8. A first print showed 10 real pairs against 2, then a fixed version showed 0 against 2. What should you write down?

Both numbers, and why the method changed: the first print used the wrong unit (every product, and pairs instead of stars). Say that you saw the higher number first, so a reader can judge whether the change was fair.

docs.title: 29 October 2026: how small a planet could we have found?
docs.text:
Field note · day 11 · about 6 min

Correction, 10 Nov 2026

An audit found that our fake-planet tests added the fake dips after the step that hides eclipses, or used a mask built from clean light. A real planet's dip is already in the light when that step runs, and the step can delete it. With the fakes put in first, the old search lost 4 to 6 of every 10 strong dips, and the loss grows as the binary gets slower (most lost dips are in 5 to 14 day binaries, because most of our data are there). So every "found X percent", "smallest planet" and "floor" number on this page is an upper limit. "No excess of real dips over noise" is not changed. The full story.

In plain words

We have searched 549 stars with Vesper and found nothing above noise. Today we asked the question that gives that result its meaning: if a planet had been there, how big would it have to be for us to catch it? We pasted thousands of fake dips into our own data and ran the whole frozen search on them. The answer is humbling. Only the biggest planets would have been caught, so "we found nothing" is a weak statement. It is still an honest one, and now it has numbers.

docs.title: What we did, and why
docs.text:
1. We checked the fill. Our "cleaned light" input fills some missing readings from the raw light. We counted: 0.67% of readings are filled, and a filled reading sits inside 8.5% of real dips and 7.8% of upside-down dips, so it affects both sides alike VERIFIED. No error was swallowed in secret. The run logs hold zero errors; the only silent skips are 21 QLP files with no safe time windows.
  2. We found a wrong name. Of the 14 first-tier dips we called "cleaned light", 10 sit on QLP's raw flux, because QLP has no cleaned column before sector 56 VERIFIED. The comparison with the upside-down copy still holds, since both sides use the same flux, but the word "cleaned" was wrong. The briefing now says so, and the code gets the new name at the next freeze.
  3. We built a test that sends fake dips through the whole chain. It pastes the same fake dip, at the same time and depth, into every file of a star-sector. Then the unchanged frozen code runs: search, checks, second look, raw-light twin, union and tiers. With nothing pasted in, it reproduces the real events in all 299 star-sectors tried, so it is the same machine.
  4. We ran 14,352 fake dips in 299 random star-sectors, 4 lengths, 6 depths, each as a dip and as a mirror bump. Even a very deep dip (18 times the noise) is seen almost every time, but only 44% to 64% end in the first tier. Half are recovered at about 11 times the 8 hour noise, which is about 8,000 parts per million for the middle star LIKELY.
  5. We compared that with the known planets. We asked the NASA Exoplanet Archive for the sizes of known circumbinary planets and worked out the deepest dip each could make. Against 8,000 ppm only Kepler-16 b clears the bar for a middle star. Against the quietest bright stars (about 3,100 ppm) roughly half of the transiting ones do.
  6. We tested the mirror. A fake dip and its mirror bump pass through the chain almost equally well: 32% against 34% LIKELY. That supports using the upside-down copy as a control, within about two points.
  7. We counted the next star list (G2). The catalogue we already had gives 895 new stars under the same rule as G1. I first guessed 1 to 4 GB of downloads. The query said about 28 GB, because every star has many sectors. I wrote my wrong guess down next to the right number.
  8. One slip of mine: I pointed the browser at a PDF link and it offered to save the file on your PC. You cancelled it and nothing was saved. The new rule: I ask before touching any file link.

docs.title: The idea behind it
docs.text:
Idea (injection and recovery): to learn what a search could find, paste fake signals of known size into real data and count how many come out. The fraction is the completeness. It must be measured through the whole chain, because a dip that is found can still be thrown out by a check.

Idea (a ceiling is information): at 18 times the noise a dip is seen 99% of the time but kept only about 55% of the time. The missing 45% is the price of the checks. A check that protects against false alarms also loses real dips, and both sides of that trade should be measured.

Idea (depth first, radius second): a planet's dip depth is its radius over the crossed star's radius, squared, times the share of light that star gives. We know neither number for a binary, and the catalogue radius describes the blend. So we report depth and length first, and planet size only as a labelled range.

Idea (a name can mislead): "cleaned light" turned out to be mostly raw QLP flux. When a label hides what is inside, count the contents.

Idea (a guess is not a measurement): my 1 to 4 GB guess was wrong by a factor of seven. A cheap query replaced it. Check before you plan around a number.

Idea (test the control, not only the data): the upside-down copy is only a fair control if every check treats it like the data. The mirror test checks that for planet-like signals.

docs.title: How you could do it yourself
docs.text:
• Print the whole recovery table from the saved rows: from the project folder run cd pipeline, then ..\.venv\Scripts\python.exe chain_recovery.py summary v7.
  • Re-run the faithfulness test: ..\.venv\Scripts\python.exe chain_recovery_test.py (a few minutes). It prints PASS lines.
  • Look up a known planet's size yourself on the NASA Exoplanet Archive and compute (planet radius over star radius) squared.

docs.title: What we found, and what we did not
docs.text:
• Found (VERIFIED, our own runs): the fill is 0.67% and acts on both sides alike; the whole chain recovers at most 44% to 64% of very deep dips; half are recovered at about 11 times the 8 hour noise; a dip and its mirror bump are recovered about equally (32% against 34%).
  • Found (VERIFIED by counting): 10 of the 14 "cleaned-light" first-tier dips are on QLP raw flux.
  • Found (LIKELY): a null on our 549 stars excludes giant planets and quiet bright stars, not typical circumbinary planets. The depths of the known ones are upper bounds, because their star's companion adds light.
  • Found (LIKELY): the flat-baseline check costs long dips most (10% of short dips, 37% of 20 hour dips), probably because the 2 day smoothing window absorbs part of a long dip. NOT TESTED.
  • Not tested: planet size from the real crossed-star radius and light share (not in our table); the 90% level (our depth grid stopped at 18 times the noise); false alarms per check set against dips lost per check; any real event. Nobody has looked at any event.
  • Uncertain: whether the saved TESS binary catalogue's periods were redone with the later sectors; how much of the 28 GB is 20 second files.

docs.title: Questions
docs.text:
1. A fake dip is seen at SNR 7 in 99% of runs but ends in the first tier 55% of the time. Where did the other 44% go?

Into the checks. Flags for data gaps, ramps, a non-flat baseline, eclipses, shared moments and repeats move a found dip to tier 2. Quote both numbers: found, and kept.

2. Why do we report dip depth before planet radius?

Depth is what we measure. Radius needs the crossed star's radius and its share of the light, and for a binary the catalogue gives neither. The radius is a range with assumptions, not a measurement.

3. Kepler-16 b makes a dip of about 14,000 ppm and Kepler-38 b about 500 ppm. Which could our search catch at 50%?

Only the first, and only around a middle star (50% needs about 8,000 ppm). The second is far below even the best case of about 3,100 ppm.

4. What does the mirror-bump test check?

Whether the checks treat a dip in the real path and a bump in the upside-down path alike. If they do, the upside-down copy is a fair control for planet-like signals. Here they differ by about two points, which is small.

5. We guessed 1 to 4 GB and the query said 28 GB. What was the mistake?

I used the sector count in the table, but the archive holds every sector TESS has released since. When a number drives a plan, measure it with the cheapest check first.

6. Why was 'cleaned light' a misleading name?

10 of the 14 dips it covers sit on QLP's raw flux column, since QLP has no cleaned column before sector 56. The label hid what was inside. Count the contents before trusting the name.

docs.title: 30 October 2026: we tried to make the filter better and learned why it will not be free
docs.text:
Field note · day 12 · about 6 min

In plain words

Since 29 October we have been asking one question: how can our filter find smaller circumbinary planets? Today we finished a long round of tests. Every idea we tried either found more fake dips as fast as it found more real ones, or found nothing new. That is a result, not a failure of effort. It tells us the filter is close to a balance: more planets caught costs more false alarms, about one for one. The choice of how many false alarms to accept is yours, not a thing to tune quietly.

docs.title: What we did, and why
docs.text:
1. We asked whether the next big step (stacking) was worth it. Stacking means adding up several transits of the same planet to see a smaller one. Before doing any work we wrote a rule down: skip it if the known planets are mostly slow and stacking reaches few of our stars. We read the NASA Exoplanet Archive: 14 transiting circumbinary planets are known, 11 of them have periods over 100 days, and the middle one is about 194 days. At that period stacking reaches only about 10% (first star list) to 19% (second list) of our stars, even in the best case. The rule said skip, so we skipped.
  2. We looked at the false alarms that get through. They are not white noise. Our nine checks stop about 98% of upside-down events, at every brightness; the 2% that get through look like short glitches. On both star lists the 3 hour box held most of them: 14 of 32 and 16 of 25.
  3. We read how a published search handles the same problem (the mono-cbp paper, Davies and others, 2026). It reaches the same conclusion: most things that pass are leftover systematics. Its extra check, that a dip must survive many smoothing settings, costs up to two thirds of the shallow long dips, the same trade we had already measured.
  4. We tested a box floor. The idea: drop the 3 hour box, the false alarms go, we gain room to loosen another check. We wrote the rule and the hope before running anything. Results on both lists: with the box gone, the false alarms did not go. They moved to the 4 hour box. The count of short-box survivors stayed at 17 on the first list and went from 20 to 16 on the second. The floor cost 7 to 8 points of recovery for 4 hour dips and bought nothing significant. Combined with the looser step check, false alarms stayed at 10 to 12 per 1,000 star-sectors against our limit of 8.
  5. We filed every result, including the failures, in the plan, the version table and a shopping list for the next version. Nothing was tuned on the results, and nobody opened a real event.

docs.title: The idea behind it
docs.text:
Idea (write the rule before the result): the stacking gate and the box-floor test were written down first, so the answer could not bend to what we wished. The gate said skip, and we skipped; the test said no gain, and we recorded no gain.

Idea (an exchange rate): for every idea that did work, the gain in real dips was about equal to the gain in false alarms. When a filter sits at a balance like that, the right question is not "which trick?" but "how many false alarms are we willing to pay for how many planets?"

Idea (where something is found is not what causes it): the false alarms were most common in the 3 hour box, so I blamed the box. But when we removed it, the same glitches were found by the next box. A count by box shows where a thing is caught first. To find the cause you must ask: if I remove this, where does it go?

Idea (check a borrowed rule's conditions): I used a published "smoothing window is three times the transit" rule in a case where its conditions did not hold (our smoothing does not mask the dip). It cost a quarter of an 8 hour dip. Read when a rule applies, not just what it says.

docs.title: How you could do it yourself
docs.text:
• Look up the periods yourself on the NASA Exoplanet Archive (filter for circumbinary, transiting) and take the median.
  • Re-run the box-floor test: from the project folder run cd pipeline, then ..\.venv\Scripts\python.exe test_vopts.py (a minute; it prints PASS lines). The full runs take hours at low priority.
  • Read the three tables in research\stage3\VESPER-VERSIONS.md and look at the last column: it is the reason each idea was not accepted.

docs.title: What we found, and what we did not
docs.text:
• Found (CONFIRMED, our own runs and the archive): stacking reaches few stars at the periods most known planets have; the false alarms that get through are short glitches; dropping the 3 hour box moves them to the 4 hour box; every option tried trades about one real gain for one false alarm.
  • Found (LIKELY): the filter is near a balance, so only new information (a physical duration limit per star, or repeat transits for the short-period planets) can improve it without a cost.
  • Not tested: a physical duration limit per star (needs star radii, a download that needs your yes); a higher bar only for the shortest boxes; the repeated-transit check for the short-period end; any real event.
  • Uncertain: how many of our binaries can show a 3 hour transit at all.

docs.title: Questions
docs.text:
1. Why did we write the stacking rule before reading the archive?

So the answer could not be shaped by what we hoped for. A rule written first is a test; a rule written after the result is a story.

2. The 3 hour box held most false alarms. Why did removing it not help?

The false alarms are short glitches, and the 4 hour box catches the same glitches. The box showed where they were found, not what made them.

3. What does 'one for one' mean here, and why does it matter?

For each extra real dip we recover we also let through about one extra false alarm. So there is no free improvement left in tuning; the number of false alarms we accept has to be decided on purpose.

4. Why is it good news that the idea failed?

We know why, we filed it so nobody repeats it, and the next step is clear. A clean, measured null is the win condition of this project.

docs.title: Later the same day: the v8 design
docs.text:
With the testing round finished, we wrote the next version. Three choices were open (how many false alarms to accept, whether to keep the shortest box, how to weigh the dip lengths). For each one I kept the rule we had written before the tests, because changing a rule after seeing which options fall just short of it is a quiet way of tuning on results. You can still change any of them before the freeze.

So v8 is the old filter plus one new check: the orbit-locked flag. A dip that repeats in another sector at exactly a whole number of the binary's own orbits, with the same length and depth, is most likely a leftover eclipse, not a planet, because a planet keeps its own clock. On the development stars it removes 49 events on 7 stars, the real-minus-control excess drops from +65 to +20, and it costs about 0.8% of planted fake planets. On the first star list it changes nothing. The check is built, tested and gives exactly the numbers we measured offline. It is not frozen yet: the freeze and the sealed stars wait for your go.

5. Why is a dip that repeats at a whole number of binary orbits suspicious?

The binary's eclipses keep the binary's clock. A planet orbits more slowly on its own clock, so its transits do not land on whole numbers of binary orbits except by chance.

Later still: you approved, and v8 is now frozen (Vesper 0.8.0, fingerprint 5f73692944aa). Before freezing we re-ran the old checks with the new flag on: 300 of 300 sample star-sectors give exactly the same events and tiers on the first star list, and all old tests pass. One old test failed first: its made-up events had no depth, which every real event has. The fix was to the test, not the filter.

docs.title: Evening: someone else did the careful part, and we read it
docs.text: Ahmed found a news story: an independent researcher, Pavel Rabtsevich, used AI agents on 126,000 TESS stars and published a possible planet (1.4 Earth radii, every 3.18 days) around TIC 4206066. We read the preprint record and two news reports before saying anything. The planet is not confirmed: TESS watches the star from 31 October to 26 November, and the result does not exist yet. The professionals' pipelines had also seen the signal earlier. What stands out is his habits: rules and dip times written first, 74 attempts to break his own result, public data and code, and "no statistical validation is claimed". Those are the habits this project already has. The full note is research/stage3/rabtsevich-literature-2026-10-30.md, and Chapter 14 has a short section on it.

docs.title: Night: a window onto the search
docs.text:
Ahmed asked to watch the search happen. We built a Search window page in the book. While a run goes, a small script counts what the search has written (stars done, dips stopped by each safety check, the self-test of fake planets, files skipped) and publishes only those counts. It never shows a real dip. For the one-time sealed search it runs in blind mode: real and upside-down dips are pooled, so nobody sees the answer before the analysis we wrote down in advance. Tested on the finished development run (3,425 star-sectors) and on a partial copy for the "running" state. Honest limit: I do not look at stars by eye; every star gets the same checks, and the page lets you watch them work.

Later that night Ahmed asked that the page update by itself, show whether the search is working, and say what is happening. The page now has a live light (running, no process found, not updating, finished), a path diagram where the working step glows, speed charts, counts by dip length and strength, a notes line from Claude, and a collapsed "for the curious" panel with the technical settings. It reads its numbers from a separate data branch on GitHub every minute, so nothing needs a tap and the book does not have to be published again for each update. We tested it with a fake run that grew while the page stayed open: the numbers changed with no reload.

Ahmed then allowed pictures of real stars and real dips on the Search window so he can learn from them. The page now draws real TESS light, 36 hours either side of an event, with the dip marked and the data gaps dashed, and says in one sentence why a stopped dip was stopped. In the sealed run the pictures are blind: real and upside-down events are mixed, the kind is not even stored in the exported file, and the labels are revealed only in the analysis we wrote down in advance. Still unpublished: event tables, candidate claims, any verdict. He also asked us to cut generic lines from the page, which is now a rule for new pages.

docs.title: Late night: getting the sealed run ready
docs.text: Ahmed approved the next step, and said not to stop before the download. Before any sealed file was fetched we wrote the permission into the locked rules as Amendment 1, so the order of events is on record: rules, freeze, approval, download. Then we built four things that touch no result. A runner that refuses to start unless the code on disk has exactly the frozen fingerprint (we tested it with the wrong switch, the wrong star set and the right one). A scorecard that prints the eight benchmark lines with their pass marks written beforehand; we tried it on the development stars, where it shows why the new orbit-locked check matters: without it the development stars look like an excess, with it they do not. The expected transits of the known planet TOI-1338 b, taken from the discovery paper's prediction table and checked cell by cell against the page, so that later we can say which of its transits our search should have caught. And a download script for the 594 sealed stars, now running in the background. The search itself has not started and waits for a separate yes.

docs.title: The sealed search: what it found (30 Oct, night)
docs.text:
Plain answer: we found nothing. Vesper 0.8.0 searched the 594 sealed stars once (6,877 star-sectors, about 50 minutes of search). The real light kept fewer dips than the upside-down copy: 26 real against 59 upside-down at the 7 bar, where noise alone predicted about 42 real. Under the rule we wrote before the run that is NO EXCESS: a measured null, not a detection.

The scorecard in short: S1 no excess. S2 false alarms 8.91 per 1,000 against a mark of 8, so FAIL on the mark, though the 95% interval (6.80 to 11.47) contains 8. S3 pass (planted dips 37.5%, planted bumps 37.3%). S4 completeness of planted dips: 41% at the 4 hour box, 47% at 8, 34% at 14, 28% at 20, close to the development slice (only the 20 hour box differs beyond both intervals: 28.0 against 21.3, in the good direction). S5 the orbit-locked flag moved 13 real events on 4 stars to tier 2 for a 0.51% cost. S6 below. S7 labels split filed. S8 all 6,877 star-sectors read.

Why real sits below upside-down: stars flare upward, and flipped a flare becomes a dip, so the upside-down light has more dips to begin with (1,044 against 741 raw at the 7 bar, ratio 1.41). The noise-expected line uses that ratio.

TOI-1338 b, the one known circumbinary planet. By the rule written before the run: 1 of the 7 strong tests found (sector 37). After the fact, and NOT part of the test (UNCERTAIN): in five later sectors (65, 89, 93, 96, 98) the search saw real events of signal-to-noise 7 to 19 that sit 0.6 to 1.4 days after the published prediction, the offset mostly growing with time. The prediction comes from a 2020 fit extrapolated years ahead, so a drifting ephemeris could explain it. These are not counted as finds. The check against a later published ephemeris is in the fix queue.

Two bugs of mine, found while reading. (1) The page code had score bands only up to 1e9. One star-sector had a dip score of 3.5e26 (its noise estimate was near zero), so the page could not read that file, counted 6,876 of 6,877 groups, never said FINISHED, and the runner waited for it and crashed after the search was done. (2) The labels report used the development noise file instead of the sealed one. Neither touched a search result; both are fixed and committed. The 3.5e26 event itself was stopped by two checks (tier 2).

New: What the search found. The Search window now opens with one plain verdict, a funnel from all dips to leads (real beside upside-down) and a card for each lead. Lesson from building it: my first version counted the first-pass files and showed real above upside-down while the scorecard said no excess. The last checks and counting only the best light curve of each star-sector explain the gap. I rebuilt it from the scorecard's own events and wrote the change into the rules as an amendment, in the open. On the sealed run it shows 6 leads against 25 upside-down copies, and says to treat them as noise until a check says otherwise.

docs.title: 31 October 2026: the search did see the known planet; our test used an old calendar
docs.text:
Field note · day 13 · about 6 min

In plain words

After the sealed search gave its clean null, we spent a day asking why it came out that way. The biggest answer: the one known planet in the stars, TOI-1338 b, was not missed as badly as the score said. We had checked the wrong dates. With the dates published later, the search saw it in 7 of 10 passes in front of its star.

docs.title: What we did, and why
docs.text:
1. We checked the known-planet test against newer papers. Our test used the transit dates predicted in 2020. A 2024 paper shows those dates drift by up to a day or more, because a second planet pulls on the first. We did not change the old score (it was written down before the run). We added a second line, marked as written afterwards.
  2. We measured what the surviving false alarms look like. Many upside-down false alarms start abruptly and recover slowly. That is the shape of a stellar flare turned upside down. Real planet transits are symmetric.
  3. We priced every safety check. For each check we asked: if we switch only this one off, how many fake planets come back, and how many true ones do we gain?
  4. We counted in stars, not events. A few stars carry many events, so counting events overstates how sure we are.
  5. We read how Kepler and ExoFOP handle the same problems (links in the findings file).

docs.title: What we found, and what we did not
docs.text:
• TOI-1338 b: 7 of 10 passes have a real dip within about 1.7 hours of the dates in the 2024 paper; 4 of the 10 were kept as strong. Four were predicted by that paper before the data existed, and all four matched. (Chance of that happening by luck: well under one in a million.)
  • Flares: about half of the false alarms that got through show the flare shape, against about one in eight of the real ones. A shape check could remove many of them at a small cost. We have not tested that cost yet.
  • Checks: the step check buys the most planets back but costs about 7 fake ones per point; three smaller checks cost about 4 times less per point. We have not tested them together.
  • What the null rules out: much less than "no planets". A single sector catches only about a quarter of 95 day transits.
  • How to report a find: the official ExoFOP site now accepts only candidates that are already published, so a find goes through a paper or a collaborator first.
  • Not found: how many human eyes are needed to beat the search, and whether the flare shape is really flares (no catalogue was compared).

docs.title: Questions
docs.text:
1. Why did we keep the old score and add a second line instead of changing it?
  2. Why is a flare a problem for the upside-down control?
  3. Why does counting stars give a more honest answer than counting events?

Answers: 1. The old score was fixed before the run; changing it afterwards would be tuning on results. 2. Turned upside down it becomes a short deep dip, which our edge checks do not catch. 3. Events from one star are not independent, so the same star counted many times looks like more evidence than it is.

Full numbers, labels and links: research/stage3/post-sealed-literature-2026-10-31.md in the repository.

docs.title: 2 November 2026: before judging a change, make sure you are comparing like with like
docs.text:
Field note · day 15 · about 7 min

In plain words

We built the eye test that decides when you may look at real candidates, and we tested a possible improvement to the search. While testing the improvement we nearly compared a new run with an old run that had been made under different conditions. A consistency check stopped us before any verdict was read. We reran the old setting under today's conditions instead.

docs.title: What we did, and why
docs.text:
1. The rehearsal (step three of the ladder to real data). Eight sessions of 20 items, in the same three-panel layout the real candidates will use. Every item is real TESS light with at most one thing hidden in it: a fake planet (clear or near the limit), a real eclipse, an instrument effect, a flare, a step, or nothing. You answer, lock, and only then see the truth. The pass line was written before the page existed.
  2. Testing it three ways before it went live. Unit checks of the arithmetic (38), a browser test at three screen sizes (73 checks), and a test that plays a whole session as your device against a copy of the cloud (12 checks). We also posted one real rehearsal round to the real cloud rules and deleted it at once, to be sure a refusal could not silently leave your answers waiting on your phone.
  3. Keeping the scores apart. Rehearsal rounds are counted on their own, so they never mix into your practice numbers.
  4. A change to the search, judged by rules written first. Three small switches (a depth limit, a fix for one broken light curve, a flare-shape check) were run on the development stars only. The accept rules were written in a plan before any run.
  5. A comparison that was not like for like. The plan assumed an older run of the development stars held the same events as a run today. Our own analysis script checked this first and refused to continue: 77 of 583 groups of one kind had different events.

docs.title: The idea behind it
docs.text: A comparison only means something if the two sides differ in one thing. Here a second thing had changed. Stars that have no data of their own in one product borrow good stretches of data from neighbouring stars in the same sector. Between the two runs we had downloaded more stars, so the list of neighbours had grown. Nothing was wrong with either run; they were just not comparable. See Chapter 15 and the new check at the end of the learning track.

docs.title: What we found, and what we did not
docs.text:
• Found: the cause of the difference (CONFIRMED: every one of the 77 changed groups borrows its windows, none of the 2,651 groups with their own windows changed).
  • Found: a rehearsal round is accepted by the cloud rules, cannot be changed or deleted from outside, and is read back with all 20 answers.
  • Study result: under the rules written first, all three switches pass on the development stars. The depth limit and the fix for the broken light curve change nothing there (they are safety guards). The flare-shape check at its most aggressive setting removes 11 of 22 false alarms (half, but only 22 of them, on 18 stars) at the cost of about 1 percentage point of the planted fake planets it recovers (38% down to about 37%). This is a development result, and nothing is frozen: the fresh star list is the clean test.
  • Not tested: Safari on a real iPhone and real touch gestures for the new page (only a simulated phone was used).
  • Not decided: whether the borrowing should be frozen per star list; this is logged as a bug (item 70) to decide before the next star list is searched.

docs.title: Questions
docs.text:
1. Why did the study stop to rerun the old setting instead of using the old run?
  2. Why were the accept rules written before the runs?
  3. Why is a good result in the rehearsal necessary but not enough?

Answers: 1. The old run had been made with a smaller list of neighbouring stars, so a difference between the runs could not be blamed on the new switches alone. 2. Rules written after seeing results can be bent to fit them. 3. The fake planets are simple shapes planted in real light; a real planet may look a little different.

Full numbers and labels: research/stage3/v9-study-results.txt, research/stage3/V9-STUDY-PLAN.md (with its addendum) and research/stage3/REHEARSAL-V1.md in the repository.

docs.title: 3 November 2026: when a frozen version refuses to freeze, believe it, then prove the extra changes do nothing
docs.text:
Field note · day 16 · about 8 min

In plain words

We got the search ready for a third list of stars. The step that freezes a version refused to freeze, because two more code files had changed since the last freeze. We did not override it. We re-ran old results through the new code on three samples of 300 star-sectors each, found two differences, traced them to a limit of our own test (not the code), fixed the test, and only then froze. We also made the text on the phone at least 14 px, and drew a first map of the planets the search could have seen.

docs.title: What we did, and why
docs.text:
1. Prepared the third list for the search (not started). The search is one-shot: it runs once, on stars it has never seen, with rules fixed first. The code had to learn the new list's file locations, periods, eclipse times and eclipse lengths. These are data paths, not rules.
  2. A fixed table of borrowed good time. Faint stars often have only one kind of light curve, which needs good-quality time stretches borrowed from neighbouring stars in the same sector and camera. The 612 stars of the third list alone would give almost none (about 1% of cases get a safe borrow). Pooling the three lists gives about 80%. We built that pool once, wrote down its fingerprint, and made the run refuse any other table.
  3. The freeze refused. The fingerprint covers eleven code files. Five differed from the old freeze: three we had changed on purpose, and two more from switches added on 2 November for a study (they stay off unless asked). We had not noticed that these had already moved the fingerprint.
  4. Proving it, three ways. The whole chain was re-run on 300 star-sectors each: the first list with the switches off, the first list with the current setting, and the second list's stored one-time search. Every event and every tier had to match the stored results.
  5. Two differences, found and explained. In the third test two events were ranked lower in the stored run. A rule says an event is doubted if it has a partner at a whole number of binary orbits in another sector. Our test looked at one sector at a time, so it could not see the partner. The code was right; the test was too narrow. We widened the test and all three passed 300 of 300.
  6. Text size. On a phone, a lot of labels, table headings and captions were 12 to 13 px. Everything readable is now at least 14 px, and a browser test fails the build if any readable text goes below that.
  7. A first reach map. For each planet size and orbital period, how likely was the search to find it? It is an upper bound (a planted fake dip is easier than a real, wandering one), so it is labelled that way.

docs.title: The idea behind it
docs.text: A fingerprint is a promise: the rules that made a result are exactly the rules we say made it. A refusal is the promise working. When it refuses, the wrong moves are to edit the fingerprint or to say the extra changes are probably harmless. The right move is to find exactly what differs, then re-run old results through the new code and look for any difference. When a test and the code disagree, find out which one is wrong before you change either.

docs.title: What we found, and what we did not
docs.text:
• Found (CONFIRMED): the new code reproduces the stored results exactly: 300 of 300 star-sectors in each of the three tests (661, 661 and 714 events).
  • Found (CONFIRMED): the borrowed-time table covers 80% of the faint star-sectors that need a borrow with the pooled lists, against 1% with the third list alone.
  • Found (CONFIRMED): the third list's stars are faint, so it tests large planets: in about two thirds of its star-sectors the smallest planet that reaches a signal of 7 in one crossing is above 10 Earth radii.
  • Not done: the search on the third list. It waits for an explicit go.
  • Not tested: whether the stated eclipse lengths in the third list's catalogue are full widths or narrower ones (UNCERTAIN; a small effect on one flag). Later the same day (audit): they are LIKELY full-width-like. Against the physics length, the third list's median is 0.50 and our first list's measured full widths give 0.38, so they are not narrower. Still not CONFIRMED, because the catalogue's own definition was not opened.

docs.title: Later the same day: what a public amateur package taught us
docs.text:
Ahmed asked what we can learn from Pavel Rabtsevich, who reported a planet candidate around the star TIC 4206066 using Claude Code and Codex. What is CONFIRMED: it is a candidate only, he claims no validation, and TESS watches the star from 31 October to 26 November 2026, so the real answer is still to come. We read his Research Note, his data package and his preregistration. Things he does that we do not do yet:

  1. A public, hashed prediction before the new data, with four outcomes (recovered, inconsistent, excluded, insufficient). A missing signal counts as excluded only if the test would have caught it at least 95% of the time.
  2. A null built with the same machinery as the real test, and a measured count of independent trials. That count made him widen his own printed limit.
  3. A second analysis in separate code by a different model. Agreement between tools was not counted as proof.
  4. A map from every printed number to a file.
  5. A wider check that the signal was not already known, with a dated sentence.
  6. Frozen library versions, so a run refuses to start in another setup.

What we do better: our search settings and a sealed set of stars are fixed before any result is seen, while his candidate was picked after looking, below his own shortlist threshold. None of the six is built yet; they are tasks T125 to T130 in the build queue (CONFIRMED from his files; the list of his 74 tests was not found). Notes: research/stage3/rabtsevich-deep-2026-11-03.md.

docs.title: Questions
docs.text:
1. Why is a refusal to freeze good news?
  2. Two events differed between the stored run and the new code. Why did we change the test and not the code?
  3. Why borrow good time from the pooled lists instead of only the third list?

Answers: 1. It shows something changed that we had not noticed; a quiet override would have hidden it. 2. The events were ranked lower in the stored run because of a rule that needs a partner in another sector; the test only looked at one sector, so it was the test that was too narrow, and widening it made all 300 match. 3. A faint star's light curve needs good-time stretches from neighbours; the third list alone has too few neighbours (about 1% of cases) and the pool has enough (about 80%).

Full numbers and labels: research/stage3/G3-PREREGISTRATION.md (Amendment 1), research/stage3/zero-diff-0.8.1.txt, zero-diff-0.8.1-c6.txt, zero-diff-0.8.1-g2-sealed-c6.txt, research/stage3/g3-union-windows.json and research/stage3/horizon-first-reach-2026-11-03.md in the repository.

docs.title: Later the same day: what your learning-track problems taught us
docs.text:
You studied three chapters from the home-screen icon and told us what got in the way: labels on almost every line, no way back, a voice that was hard to follow and formulas that looked odd. We counted: the labels are the book's evidence chips, 125 of them in the 15 chapters and about 8 per 1000 words in the first three. The icon opens the book as a stand-alone app, and such an app has no browser Back button (the book's setup says so; your phone itself is not yet tested). The formulas are plain text because the book has no formula renderer.

The lesson: checking a claim and learning an idea are two different jobs, so the check belongs on its own page and the reading page should stay clear of it. We keep the facts register exactly as it is and plan to move the labels out of the reading (the plan is in research/stage3/LEARNING-SPACE-PROPOSAL-2026-11-03.md; nothing is built yet).

One more thing the audit found: Level 5 check 4 quotes 82.7% as if it were how much of a strong planet's signal our search catches. It is only the share of found dips that pass four of the checks, and only 72% were found at all. The correction is listed for you to approve and has not been made yet.

You also asked for an exam for the second key, to take once the track is done: it is written down as the specification research/stage3/KEYSTONE-EXAM-SPEC-2026-11-03.md, not built.

docs.title: Early on 4 November: what the Search window shows before a search starts
docs.text:
Ahmed asked for the Search window to be made ready for the G3 search. Four lessons came out of it. 1. A page needs a "not started" state. Before, it could only say running, stalled or finished. Now it can say a campaign is prepared and nothing is running, and it never pulses in that state. 2. A one-shot test is watched through counts only. The G3 list is an untouched test, so the page shows totals, no pictures, no star list and no per-star counts while it runs. Looking at individual events before the rules for reading them are used is how bias gets in. 3. Two samples are not one funnel. For the finished G2 run the page showed 12,261 event records in one place and 2,764 detections in another. The first counts every dip record in every product and pass; the second is the scorecard's sample. They answer different questions. 4. "First stop" is a way of counting, not the order the machine works in. Every dip is tested against all the checks. The page files it under the first listed flag that fired, so the rows add up. The page now lists eight checks and says so; it used to say nine, which counted the "no flag" row.

We also saved the exact library versions of the machine before the search, so the result can be rebuilt later. Full record: research/stage3/SEARCH-WINDOW-2-PROPOSAL-2026-11-04.md in the repository.

docs.title: 4 November 2026: the G3 search ran once and found nothing, and what that does and does not mean
docs.text:
Field note · day 17 · about 8 min

Correction, 10 Nov 2026

An audit found that our fake-planet tests added the fake dips after the step that hides eclipses, or used a mask built from clean light. A real planet's dip is already in the light when that step runs, and the step can delete it. With the fakes put in first, the old search lost 4 to 6 of every 10 strong dips, and the loss grows as the binary gets slower (most lost dips are in 5 to 14 day binaries, because most of our data are there). So every "found X percent", "smallest planet" and "floor" number on this page is an upper limit. "No excess of real dips over noise" is not changed. The full story.

In plain words

We ran the third and last test search, once, on 611 stars it had never seen. It took 8 minutes. It found no more real dips than random noise would give, so there is no excess and no lead. That is the clean null we aimed for. It is not proof that these stars have no planets: the stars are faint, so the search could only have seen large ones.

docs.title: What we did, and why
docs.text:
1. Ran the search once. The rules had been frozen and committed first (Vesper 0.8.1), so nothing could be tuned after seeing a result. The go came from Ahmed at about 01:09; the search ran from 01:15 to 01:20 on 8 workers.
  2. Scored it with the rules written before. The test counts real dips against dips found in the flipped (upside-down) light, which is the noise control, and asks whether the real count is clearly higher than the noise predicts.
  3. Measured what it could have seen. We planted fake dips of known depth into 300 random star-sectors and counted how many came out the other end (completeness).
  4. Looked at no individual star. The page showed counts only while it ran, and the result was read from totals.

docs.title: What we found, and what we did not
docs.text:
• Found (CONFIRMED): no excess. At the main bar (signal-to-noise 7) there were 18 real dips against 31 upside-down ones, and noise alone predicts 23.5 real. Real was below the noise expectation at all four bars. The most the data allow is about 8 real dips above noise (95%).
  • Found (CONFIRMED): the false-alarm line misses its mark again. 9.34 false alarms per 1,000 star-sectors against a mark of 8 or fewer (the earlier run gave 8.91). The interval, 6.39 to 13.19, includes the mark, so it is a miss by a small margin, twice in a row.
  • Found (CONFIRMED): completeness is modest. A planted dip lasting 8 hours was found and kept 44% of the time overall, and 60% at the deepest setting. A Jupiter-size dip (10,000 ppm) is kept about 60% of the time; a dip like TOI-1338 b's, about 6%; a 4-Earth-radius one, about 3%.
  • Found (CONFIRMED): 14% of the light-curve reads could not be searched (784 of 5,634), because no safe good-time windows were available for them.
  • Not tested: a real planet. None of these stars is a known circumbinary host, so there was nothing to recover.
  • Uncertain: the exact planet-rate limits. They assume a 1 solar-radius star and no dilution; the real star sizes are not in yet.

docs.title: Three lessons
docs.text:
1. "Fewer real dips than noise" is still "consistent with zero". The real count came out 5 below the noise expectation, but the 95% range runs from 19 below to 11 above. We read it as no excess, not as a deficit.
  2. A null is only as strong as what the search could see. The same result means different things for a Jupiter and for a small planet. The completeness table is part of the answer, not a footnote.
  3. Check the machine a minute after launch. The page feed did not start at first, because a text label with spaces was split into pieces. We found it within minutes because we looked. The fix is a rule: after every launch, check the feed is alive.

docs.title: Questions
docs.text:
1. Why is "no excess" different from "no planets"?
  2. The real count was lower than the noise expectation. Why do we not say real dips are rarer than noise?
  3. Why do we plant fake dips into the data?

Answers: 1. No excess says the real count was not higher than noise. It says nothing about planets the search could not see, such as small ones around faint stars. 2. The difference is smaller than the scatter, so it is consistent with zero. 3. It is the only way to measure how often a real dip of a known size would survive every step.

Full numbers and labels: research/stage3/G3-RESULT-2026-11-04.md, benchmark-g3-g3.txt and scorecard-plus-g3.txt in the repository.

docs.title: Night addition: where the next list comes from
docs.text:
Written the same night, after the Census plan. Nothing was searched; we only counted and checked our own numbers.

  • Found (CONFIRMED): there is a lot of unlisted fuel. TESS watched 476,784 different stars at two-minute cadence in sectors 27 to 109. Of these, 364,656 (258,858 at magnitude 13.5 or brighter) were never two-minute targets in sectors 1 to 26, the sectors the published eclipsing-binary list covers. No list names the eclipsing binaries among them.
  • Found (LIKELY, rough): at the share the published list found (1.97% of stars), those bright new stars would hold about 5,100 eclipsing binaries, and about 1,000 of the type we searched in G2 (long period, detached, bright). The error is at least a factor of 2.
  • Found (CONFIRMED): the reads we could not search are a supply problem. The 784 unsearched reads are 16% of the star-sectors. The share is 4% in sectors 1 to 26, 27% in sectors 27 to 55 and 18% after, because our safe-window borrowing needs nearby two-minute stars and we only have them where a list exists. Searching them would have added only about 8% to the reach.
  • Found (CONFIRMED and UNCERTAIN): our reach map is too generous. If the Kepler rate of 10% held, our three searches should have found 13 to 22 planets by the map as it stands, and they found none. That cannot be taken at face value: the map counts the chance that a transit falls in the observed days but not the chance that the planet transits at all. A rough cross-check against Kepler's own numbers says the map is too high by several times. How much is NOT tested.
  • Found (LIKELY, corrected 6 Nov): the size that matters. With the corrected geometry factor (see the evening addition), about 1,400 bright G2-type stars would add about half to our evidence, and about 3,000 would roughly double it.
  • Found (LIKELY, corrected 6 Nov): the missing factor is about 0.1 to 0.16 for planets at 77 to 139 days. My first probe (4 Nov) used each star's eclipse width and gave 0.05 to 0.2, with a tilt rule on top. An independent audit on 6 Nov showed that both parts were wrong (see the evening addition). The corrected rule needs only the binary's period. With it, our four searches expected about 1.5 to 3.3 planets at Kepler's rate and found none, which happens by chance 4% to 23% of the time. So the null is consistent with Kepler's rate and cannot test it. This holds with the stability limit that the known planets obey. The size of the companion star is the biggest unknown.
  • Found (CONFIRMED): fetching the light is cheaper than G3 made it look. A public Amazon bucket gave 3 files a second with 8 threads, 1.8 MB a file. G3's download ran for 21 hours of wall clock, but about 20 of them were a stall: it hit a server time-out after 410 of 612 stars, sat idle until it was restarted the next night, and the restart finished the last 202 stars in about 10 minutes. The real work was about an hour and a quarter. All 5,193 new bright stars with 8 or more sectors would take about 7 hours and 135 GB.
  • Not tested: the geometry rule on the known Kepler planets themselves (the 6 Nov audit checked the rule by algebra and a 3D simulation), and a larger fetch run. Both come before any new star list is sized.

docs.title: Three more lessons
docs.text:
1. A limit needs every factor in it. A map of what a search could see is only an upper bound until it includes the chance that a planet transits at all. Quote it as an upper bound until then.
  2. When the data feeding a rule come from a list, the rule fails where the list ends. The borrowed windows came from our own stars, which come from catalogues that stop at sector 26. The gap shows up exactly after that sector.
  3. A slow download can be a stall, not the size. G3 took 21 hours of wall clock but was working for about an hour and a quarter; the rest was a time-out that nobody noticed. The same kind of file from a public bucket moves at 5 MB a second. Measure the route on a few files, and make a download shout when it stops, before you plan around the hours.

docs.title: More questions
docs.text:
1. Why can we not yet quote the reach numbers as limits on planets?
  2. Why were more reads lost after sector 26 than before it?
  3. Why did G3 take 21 hours to download 2.2 GB when the real work took about an hour?

Answers: 4. The map leaves out the chance that a planet transits at all, so it is too high; a corrected rule puts the missing factor at roughly 0.1 to 0.16 for planets at 77 to 139 days. 5. The safe good-time windows are borrowed from nearby two-minute stars, and our two-minute stars come from lists that stop at sector 26. 6. A stall, not the size: the download hit a time-out, sat idle for about 20 hours before it was restarted, and the restart finished in 10 minutes; a public bucket moves the same kind of file at a similar speed.

docs.title: Morning addition: does the shape of a dip matter?
docs.text:
• Found (CONFIRMED): yes, a little for real planets and a lot for odd shapes. Our planted dips were flat-bottomed with short slopes. We replanted the same dips in other shapes through the same untouched search. A dip with long rounded slopes was kept 21.5% of the time against 30.5% for our flat-bottomed one. A dip shaped like a real planet crossing a star (the star is darker at its edge, the planet is a round disc) was kept 27.1% to 27.8% of the time, about 3 points or a tenth less.
  • Found (LIKELY): our quoted completeness is about a tenth too high. The search matches a box shape, and a rounder dip fits a box worse. The loss is biggest for shallow and short dips, and it disappears for loud ones.

  • Not tested: other planet sizes, grazing crossings, and the way a circumbinary planet's speed changes during a crossing.

  • A planted signal has a shape, and the shape is a choice. Check the answer for two or three shapes before you trust a completeness number; the realistic one moved ours by about a tenth.

  • Why did the completeness number fall when we planted rounder dips? Answer: the search slides a box along the light; a rounder dip fits the box less well, so more of the shallow ones slip below the line.

docs.title: Evening addition (6 Nov): a second model checked my work and found two errors
docs.text:
• Found (CONFIRMED): two of my own results were wrong. The tilt test counted planets that would transit after years of slow wobble, but one sector is a snapshot, and in a snapshot a small tilt does not change the chance (a computer simulation of 3,000 binaries gave 0.135 flat, against 0.124 to 0.143 with 1 to 3 degrees of tilt). The width method needed each eclipse width to be right to about 1%, and ours are off by 10% to 30%, so it mostly counted stars whose width had been clipped to zero. The "about 1% chance in the most optimistic corner" idea is withdrawn.
  • Found (CONFIRMED): the rest held. The geometry condition itself is right (the auditor derived it again from scratch and a simulation agreed), and every headline number in the earlier notes recomputed from the saved outputs. Four wording slips of mine were fixed.
  • Found (LIKELY): Census adds less than I first said. 1,400 bright G2-type stars add about half to our evidence, not double it; about 3,000 would double it.

  • Not tested: unequal star masses, eccentric binaries, transits of the second star and planets that are not in the binary's plane.

  • Have a different mind check your work, and then check the checker. A second model, given only the files and a written brief, found two errors I had not seen. I re-ran its scripts and got the same output before I accepted anything. The corrected numbers changed, the plain message did not.

  • Why did I re-run the auditor's scripts instead of just trusting its report? Answer: a report is a claim. The scripts were small and seeded, so running them again cost almost nothing and turned its findings from claims into reproduced results.

Numbers and labels: research/stage3/CENSUS-STEP1-COUNTS-2026-11-04.md, Q5-LOST-READS-2026-11-04.md and Q1-EXPECTED-PLANETS-2026-11-04.md in the repository. The shape test is in FIX28-SHAPE-TEST-2026-11-04.md. The audit is OPUS-TRIAL-AUDIT-2026-11-06.md; the corrected numbers are Q1 UPDATE 6.

docs.title: 10 November 2026: our eclipse mask was deleting planets, and our tests could not see it
docs.text:
Field note · day 23 · about 8 min

In plain words

An outside audit found a flaw in how we tested our own search. The step that hides the stars' eclipses can also hide a planet's dip, and every fake-planet test we ran skipped that step's damage. When we hid the fakes the way a real planet would be hidden, the old search lost 4 to 6 of every 10 strong dips. Our searches still show no excess of real dips over noise. What they rule out is much less than we wrote.

docs.title: What we found
docs.text:
1. The mask. Before searching, the old search cuts out the eclipses. It finds them by folding one sector of light on the binary's period and cutting the parts of the cycle that are low. In a slow binary each part of the cycle is seen once per sector, so a planet's dip looks like an eclipse and is cut with them.
  2. Our tests skipped it. The fake-planet tests either built the mask from clean light, or added the fake dip after the mask. A real planet is in the light when the mask is built. So the tests never saw the loss.
  3. Measured the right way. We put fake dips into real light before the mask and counted what survived (1,774 sampled files from the second and third star lists, 1,660 usable, one fake per file and size). In the second list, strong dips (25 times the noise, 8 hours long) survived like this:
Binary period 5 to 10 d 10 to 14 d 14 to 20 d 20 to 27 d over 27 d Found, fake added after the mask (old test) 1.00 1.00 1.00 1.00 0.99 Found, fake added before the mask (like a real planet) 0.66 0.26 0.07 0.01 0.02
  1. Our own planet star. On TOI-1338's 40 sectors, fakes of the three larger sizes together were found 0.58 of the time before the mask against 0.95 after. A 25-times-noise, 8-hour dip: 0.28 against 1.00.
  2. A published planet. In one data set of TIC 172900988 b, both of its published dips are deleted by the old mask.
  3. Mirror bumps are not lost. The upside-down copy of the light is a fair control only if both versions are treated alike. The old mask cuts dips and not bumps, so the control was unfair in slow binaries.
  4. We broke our own test on purpose to check it can fail. It did, each time.

docs.title: What the professionals do
docs.text: The two closest published searches (STANLEY, and a 2026 search for single transits in TESS binaries) do not guess the eclipses from the light. They read each binary's timetable from a catalogue: period, time of the eclipse, how long it lasts, and cut only those hours. That does not depend on the planet, so a planet cannot be mistaken for an eclipse.

docs.title: What we tried
docs.text:
• Catalogue timetable only. Planted dips survive (98 to 100 out of 100 in both lists). But eclipses missing from the timetable leak through, and only the real light shows them: about twice as many real dips as upside-down ones, so the control is no longer fair.
  • Timetable plus "a dip that comes back at the same point of the cycle is an eclipse". Planted dips survive (99 out of 100), and the control is fair again for binaries under about 13 days. Slow binaries still leak. A separate step that removes recurring events across sectors is being tested.

docs.title: What this changes
docs.text:
• Every "found X percent", "smallest planet" and "floor of 6 Earth radii" number in this book was measured the old way. Read it as an upper limit. Each page where it appears now carries a correction.
  • Not changed: our three searches found no excess of real dips over noise. That still stands.
  • What the nulls can exclude: much less than we wrote, above all for binaries slower than about 14 days.
  • Next: finish the new mask, freeze it as a new version, and search the light we already have again. Real events stay private.

docs.title: Check yourself
docs.text:
1. Why can the old mask delete a planet's dip in a slow binary but not in a fast one? (Each part of the cycle is seen once per sector, so a one-off dip looks like an eclipse.)
  2. Why did the old tests not notice? (They added the fake dips after the mask, or built the mask from light without the fake.)
  3. Why is the upside-down light no longer a fair control with the old mask? (It cuts dips but leaves bumps.)

docs.title: 11 November 2026: we searched the hidden light again, found nothing, and learned how to read that
docs.text:
Field note · day 24 · about 8 min

In plain words

We searched the light our old filter used to throw away, in 803 binary stars that were never used to design anything. The real dips did not beat the upside-down control. Nothing to check and no leads. The most useful part came before the search: our own test would have shouted "excess" even with no planet in the sky, and we caught it in time.

docs.title: What we found
docs.text:
1. The new filter keeps the light. It is frozen as Petrova 1.0.0 (the new name for Vesper). Switched off, it gives exactly the old answers (300 of 300 test star-sectors, three ways). Planted fake dips and fake bumps survive it as well as they survive without it.
  2. The old test would have lied. In the light the old filter deleted, which sits next to the binary's own eclipses, real dips outnumber upside-down dips 2 to 4 times even after the new mask (on the design stars: 33 against 8 in one list, 65 against 33 in the other). In light both filters keep, the two sides are balanced (10 against 13). The likely cause is the leftover edges of the eclipses: they only dip, they never bump, so they only show on the real side.
  3. So we fixed the rule first, in writing. The new stars are compared with the design stars, bin by bin of binary period, and the rule was committed before any new star was read.
  4. The answer. New stars, real against upside-down strong dips in the recovered light: 16 against 6 in the third list, 32 against 13 in the second. That is the same imbalance as on the design stars. Chance of seeing this if nothing new is there: 0.41 and 0.31. The mark was 0.005. No excess.
  5. How big a miss would we have noticed? Only an excess of about 5 times (third list) and about 3.3 to 3.7 times (second list) the expected count. (Corrected 13 Nov 2026: the first figure for the second list, 2.7, came from a simpler test than the one that gave the verdict; an outside re-check with the right test gave 3.3 to 3.7.) About 4 in 10 planted strong dips survive the whole chain, and that is measured only in light the mask kept.
  6. Where the stars are. Of the 803 new stars, only 91 rows are slow binaries (14 days or more). The other 335 slow binaries that were never used for design are in the Kepler list (G1), which has no eclipse widths yet and was not searched.

docs.title: What this changes
docs.text:
• Our fourth search is a clean null for binaries of 5 to 14 days in the light the old filter deleted, with the limits above. For slow binaries the question is still open.
  • A null has a size. Always read the "how big an excess would show" line beside it.
  • The control is only fair if both sides are treated alike. Near eclipses they were not, and the fix was to compare like with like.
  • Next: get the eclipse widths for the Kepler list and search it; then a filter that knows the binary phase, so the leftover edges cannot pass as dips.

docs.title: Check yourself
docs.text:
1. Why must a control treat both sides alike? (Otherwise a difference between them can come from the control, not from the sky.)
  2. Why compare new stars with design stars instead of using a formula? (The imbalance is real and has no formula; the design stars measure it.)
  3. Why does "no excess" not mean "no planets"? (Only an excess above the power line would have been seen, and the completeness is about 4 in 10.)
  4. Why does it matter where the slow binaries are? (The old filter hurt them most, and most of the unseen ones are in a list we did not search.)

docs.title: 14 November 2026: the spacecraft's own hiccups, and a blind spot in our fairness check
docs.text:
Field note · day 27 · about 6 min

In plain words

Every few days TESS fires its thrusters to slow its spinning wheels (a momentum dump). For about a day before that, its pointing wobbles more and more, so a little of each star's light spills outside the box we measure it in. That makes a small dip that looks like a planet. Our upside-down check cannot see these fake dips, because a wobble only ever loses light: it never makes a bump.

docs.title: What we found
docs.text:
1. A known-events flag, adopted. NASA's sector notes list 19 moments when the telescope misbehaved (pointing shifts, tests, heater changes). Holding events that touch them costs 2 of about 1,100 test planets and removes 4 upside-down and 2 real false alarms. Codex checked it with its own code and got the same numbers. Ahmed adopted it for the next filter version.
  2. A rule that passes every test and is still not safe. Judging dips near dumps by their shape (is the light around them even?) lifts our planet score to 49.98%, with no extra upside-down alarms. But it lets back in 30 real events against only 4 upside-down ones, and 23 of the 30 sit just before a dump. The papers say why: the wobble grows before each dump (Vanderburg 2019) and lingers for hours after it (Eisner 2019).
  3. The lesson. A pass rule is only as good as its meter. Our false-alarm meter is the upside-down copy of the light, and it is blind to anything that only makes dips. So the rule waits for Fable on Monday, and Codex is measuring exactly where around a dump the fake dips appear.
  4. Equal eclipses fool a period search. Codex tried to time every binary's eclipses from TESS itself. It failed on stars whose two eclipses look alike: it saw an eclipse every half orbit and called that the period (13 of 58 control stars). On the right period the timing was good to about a minute and a half. The fix is to compare alternate eclipses before halving.

New word: aperture loss, light from the star falling outside the pixels we add up, so the star looks fainter than it is.

docs.title: Check yourself
docs.text:
1. Why can the upside-down copy not catch a dump artefact? (A wobble only removes light from the aperture, so it makes dips and never bumps.)
  2. Why is "passes every test" not enough? (The tests share one meter; if the meter is blind to an effect, every test is too.)
  3. Why does a binary with two equal eclipses look like it has half its period? (Each half orbit shows an identical dip, so folding at half the period lines them all up.)

docs.title: Lab 0: your workbench
docs.text:
Lab · at your PC · about 10 min · Level L0

In plain words

Before you can look at stars yourself, your PC needs the right tools: Python (a programming language) and a few astronomy toolkits. They're already installed in the project folder on D:. In this lab you open a terminal, run one check, and read what it tells you.

Goal: run your first command and confirm the workbench is ready.

docs.title: What you need to know first
docs.text:
• A terminal is a window where you type commands instead of clicking. On Windows it's called PowerShell.
  • Python runs our scripts. The project has its own copy, with all the toolkits, at D:\second-sun\.venv. A copy like this is called a virtual environment: it keeps the project's tools separate from everything else on your PC.
  • Why D:? Your C: drive is nearly full. Every lab keeps downloads and temporary files on D:. The file labs/_env.py, which every lab loads first, makes sure of that.

The toolkits you'll meet:

You type a star's name. This is exactly how I start with any star.

The commands, when you are at your PC 
cd D:\second-sun

It takes about 20 seconds, because it's asking NASA's servers over the internet.

docs.title: Reading it line by line
docs.text:
• Three names, one star. TIC is TESS's catalogue number, KIC is Kepler's, and the Gaia number is from the European star map (Chapter 1). Our G1 list stores the KIC and the TIC for every star.
  • Position. RA and Dec are the sky's longitude and latitude. Dec +51.8° puts Kepler-16 in the northern sky, in the constellation Cygnus, inside Kepler's old field.
  • TESS magnitude 10.94. About 100 times too faint to see with your eyes (Chapter 1), but bright for TESS. Our G1 list goes down to 13.5.
  • 4018 K, 0.77 Suns. The catalogue treats the light as one star. Kepler-16 is really two stars too close together to separate, so these are blended values.
  • Neighbours. A TESS pixel is 21 arcseconds wide VERIFIED, so a star within 1 arcminute shares pixels with ours. Four neighbours bright enough to matter means a dip could come from one of them. That's why Chapter 11 exists.
  • 94 light curves. Six different teams turned the same TESS pictures into light curves. SPOC is NASA's own and the best. QLP is MIT's, made for many more stars (Chapter 3). SPOC has 26 files for 17 sectors because some sectors have both a 2-minute and a 20-second version.
  • Sectors 14 to 83, with gaps. TESS came back to this part of the sky in 2019, 2020, 2021, 2022, and from late 2023 through 2024 (years checked in the archive's search table).

docs.title: How the script works
docs.text:
Open labs\lab1_name_to_number.py in Notepad and follow along:

  1. Catalogs.query_object(name, radius=2/60, catalog="TIC") asks for every TIC star within 2 arcminutes of the name's position.
  2. It sorts them by distance and takes the closest: our star. The others are the neighbours.
  3. lk.search_lightcurve(f"TIC {star['ID']}") asks MAST which light curves exist, and the loop groups them by team.

docs.text:
The commands, when you are at your PC 
cd D:\second-sun
.\.venv\Scripts\python.exe labs\lab2_get_the_data.py "Kepler-16" 82

The 82 is the sector. Downloads go to D:\second-sun\data\labs (never C:). If the file is already there, it isn't downloaded again.

docs.title: Reading it
docs.text:
The file name packs in the facts: tess2024223182411 is when the data was processed (year 2024, day 223), s0082 is the sector, 0000000299096355 is the TIC number, and _lc means light curve.

The file format is FITS, astronomy's standard since 1981. A FITS file has a header (labels: which star, which camera) and tables (the data).

The header says this star fell on camera 3, chip (CCD) 4. Stars on the same chip share spacecraft problems, which is how the QLP fix borrows good time windows from neighbours (Chapter 3).

The columns you'll use most:

Column Meaning TIME when, in BTJD: days since a fixed moment in 2014 (BJD 2457000). BTJD 3533 is August 2024 SAP_FLUX raw brightness: all the light in the star's pixels, in electrons per second PDCSAP_FLUX cleaned brightness: NASA removed known spacecraft effects. We use this first ..._ERR the expected noise on each measurement QUALITY a warning number; 0 means fine (see below) MOM_CENTR1/2 where the star's light centre sits on the chip; it moves if the telescope wobbles SAP_BKG the background sky light that was subtracted

18,619 cadences. A cadence is one measurement. 25.9 days × 720 per day (one every 2 minutes) is about 18,650, so almost none are missing.

PDCSAP is missing on 482 rows: exactly the 482 flagged ones (checked row by row). NASA blanks the cleaned flux where it doesn't trust the data.

The QUALITY number is a set of switches added together. Each switch is a power of 2:

Value Name (from lightkurve) Meaning 8 Earth point the spacecraft turned toward Earth to send data home 16 Argabrightening a sudden glow across the whole camera (cause uncertain) 32 Desaturation event momentum dump: thrusters fired VERIFIED 128 Manual exclude NASA's team marked these by hand 2048, 4096 Straylight scattered light from Earth or Moon (not in this file; common in others)

This file contains the values 8, 16, 32, 40, 128 and 160 (checked by script). A value of 40 means 32 + 8: a thruster firing and an Earth-point moment; 160 is 128 + 32. The 16 momentum-dump cadences matter: on 20 October our first G1 dip turned out to be the telescope wobbling just before one (Chapter 10).

docs.title: Reading the picture
docs.text:
• The deep drop near BTJD 3552 is the two stars eclipsing each other: the small star passes in front of the big one. It's about 8 to 12% deep, far deeper than any planet. The binary's period is 41.08 days, so a 26-day sector catches at most one of each kind.
  • Raw vs cleaned. The raw curve drifts and jumps at each gap. NASA's cleaning flattens those drifts, but look just after the eclipse: the cleaned curve spikes up where the raw one doesn't. Cleaning can create problems as well as remove them.
  • The small bump near 3544 in the raw data is gone in the cleaned data. Something on the camera, not the star.
  • The red lines are thruster firings, about every 6 days VERIFIED. One sits right at the end of the eclipse, exactly where the cleaned curve spikes: two problems in one place, so that stretch needs care.

docs.title: Reading the table
docs.text:
• 2 min: one measurement wobbles by about 2,000 ppm (0.2%).
  • "If white" is what averaging should give if every wobble were independent: divide by √N (Chapter 7).
  • Measured stays much higher. Over 1 hour it's 908 ppm, not 368. Slow wobbles don't average away. That's red noise, and it's why a 5-hour planet dip of 1,000 ppm would be hard to see here.

Why this lab corrected our own number

While building this lab I found that an earlier estimate of Kepler-16's one-hour noise (236 ppm) used a quick method that flattens away most of the slow wobble. The real figure for our search is about 900 ppm VERIFIED. Chapter 7 tells the story; it's logged in the mistakes register.

docs.text:
1. Reads the file and finds the binary's period in our G1 list by the TIC number.
  2. Plots raw and cleaned brightness, divided by their middle value so 1.0 means "normal".
  3. Keeps only quality-0 rows, flattens slow trends with the same 2-day filter our detector uses, and masks the eclipses.
  4. For each bin size, averages groups of points and measures the spread with a robust method (it ignores a few wild points).

• The warning line: 37% of this sector is thrown away by the quality filter. That's a lot, and it's mostly scattered light (Lab 2's bits 2048 and 4096). Compass flagged this: some of that data could be kept with a warning instead. It's on the list.

docs.title: Lab 5: two suns up close
docs.text:
Lab · at your PC · about 15 min · Level L4 · after Chapter 6

In plain words

You take one month of TOI-1338 data and "fold" it: cut it into 14.6-day pieces (one orbit of the two stars) and stack them. Both eclipses line up and become easy to see and measure. This is how our search finds and hides the stars' own eclipses before looking for a planet.

Goal: see both eclipses of a real binary, measure them, and see what gets masked.

docs.title: What you should see
docs.text:
Folded 25321 measurements at P = 14.6086 d. Eclipses found: 2
  phase 0.509: depth 5.67%, width about 5.3 h
  phase 0.963: depth 0.32%, width about 5.3 h
Second eclipse comes 0.453 of an orbit after the first (0.500 would mean a circular orbit)
Masked before searching: 15.1% of the data
Picture saved: D:\second-sun\labs\out\lab5_toi1338_fold.png
TOI-1338, sector 98, folded at 14.6086 days, from your PC VERIFIED. Red: masked. Middle: the primary eclipse. Right: the secondary.

docs.text:
The commands, when you are at your PC 
cd D:\second-sun
.\.venv\Scripts\python.exe labs\lab5_two_suns.py

docs.title: Reading it
docs.text:
• Phase is where in the stars' orbit a measurement sits, from 0 to 1. Folding puts all orbits on top of each other.
  • The deep eclipse (phase 0.509): the small star passes in front of the big one and blocks about 6% of the light at the bottom. The script reports 5.67%, the typical value inside the masked stretch. With Chapter 2's formula, √0.06 ≈ 0.24: the small star is about a quarter of the big one's size.
  • The shallow eclipse (phase 0.963): the big star hides the small, faint one. Only 0.3% of the light disappears, because the small star gives so little light.
  • 0.453, not 0.5: the orbit is stretched (Chapter 6).
  • The gap from phase 0.02 to 0.35. Look at the picture: almost no data there. The quality filter dropped 37% of this sector (Lab 4), mostly scattered light that returns once per TESS orbit. TESS's own orbit (13.7 days) is close to the stars' 14.6 days, so the dropped stretches likely keep landing on the same part of the stars' orbit. A planet crossing during that part of the orbit would be invisible in this sector.
  • 15.1% masked: each eclipse plus a safety margin of 1.5 times its width on both sides. Any planet crossing in there is lost to the search (Chapter 9: about 1 in 11).

docs.title: How the script works
docs.text:
1. eclipse_mask_auto() (in pipeline/detect_v2.py) folds at the period, takes the middle value in 600 phase slices, and flags slices more than 4 times the noise below normal. Each flagged run is an eclipse.
  2. The script measures each eclipse's typical depth, its phase and its width, then draws the fold and two zooms.

docs.title: Lab 6: hide your own fake planets
docs.text:
Lab · at your PC · about 20 min (the script runs 3 to 5 minutes) · Level L5 · after Chapter 9

Correction, 10 Nov 2026

An audit found that our fake-planet tests added the fake dips after the step that hides eclipses, or used a mask built from clean light. A real planet's dip is already in the light when that step runs, and the step can delete it. With the fakes put in first, the old search lost 4 to 6 of every 10 strong dips, and the loss grows as the binary gets slower (most lost dips are in 5 to 14 day binaries, because most of our data are there). So every "found X percent", "smallest planet" and "floor" number on this page is an upper limit. "No excess of real dips over noise" is not changed. The full story.

In plain words

You hide 20 fake planets (5 sizes, 4 places each) in real TOI-1338 data and run our search on every one. The table shows which were found, and how much of each dip survived our cleaning. You've just measured what our search can see.

Goal: run an injection and recovery test yourself, and read its result.
